claims.text: Atomic-scale disorder is the primary governor of superconducting transition temperature in high-entropy superconducting alloys.
Greater atomic-scale disorder enhances electron-phonon coupling.
Greater atomic-scale disorder increases electron scattering.
Greater atomic-scale disorder softens phonon modes.
The random distribution of multiple principal elements gives the cast HEA a high level of intrinsic lattice disorder.
Controlled annealing reduces lattice disorder by promoting short-range ordering relative to a quenched baseline.
Rapid quenching preserves a higher level of atomic-scale disorder than annealing followed by slow cooling.
The degree of lattice disorder or short-range order modulates the electron-scattering rate.
The degree of lattice disorder or short-range order modulates phonon softening.
Enhanced electron-phonon coupling in the disordered lattice raises Tc.
Reducing disorder through annealing diminishes electron scattering and electron-phonon coupling.
Annealed, less-disordered samples will have a lower Tc than quenched, more-disordered samples.
The proposed relationship is limited to HEAs in which electron-phonon coupling is relevant and disorder is the dominant influence on Tc.
The relationship may not apply when magnetic impurities, granularity, or non-electron-phonon factors dominate superconductivity.
Changes in grain boundaries and other microstructural features may confound the inferred effect of disorder on Tc.
A failure of reduced-disorder annealed samples to show a statistically significant lower Tc than quenched samples would falsify the hypothesis.
